[0] everyday_reading (E): In everyday language a label tells you what a thing is (a jar labelled 'sugar' holds sugar), so novices expect a variable called max to hold the maximum. Java gives names no meaning: conventions exist only for human readers, and only assignments decide values.
[1] misconception (M) -> NameGivesMeaning: wrong rule: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it. Right rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> NameGivesMeaning: Points to LT (names carry no meaning at run time, so trace by values). Applied unevenly, a student traces values for most variables but assumes that largest is larger than smallest because of its name. (here mixing in: "Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it")

[0] names_the_element (N): Naming convention: a style rule (not a language rule) for choosing identifiers. Variables and methods use lowerCamelCase, classes UpperCamelCase, constants UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES, and names describe meaning.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Variable names begin with a lowercase letter and capitalize each later word (firstName). Class names begin with a capital. Constants are all uppercase with _ between words. Names should indicate what the variable means.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Conventions have no execution order: the compiler checks only that an identifier is legal and declared, never whether it follows convention.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A program's output does not depend on its names: renaming total to t everywhere gives identical results.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Following or breaking a convention changes no state; it only changes how readable the code is.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each variable's name should describe what it holds (count, sum, maxSoFar). Single letters suit only short-lived loop indices.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Constants are written in ALL_CAPS with underscores, which sets them apart from lowerCamelCase variables and signals that they never change.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Good names make each variable's role visible (sum for a gatherer, count for a counter, max for a most-wanted holder, i for a stepper), so a reader can recognize the plan without tracing.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> NameGivesMeaning: Renaming consistently keeps the program's meaning, because what it computes does not depend on names. A misleading name (max holding a minimum) still compiles and runs the same, but readers draw wrong conclusions.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Apply the conventions to every name you write. Short names fit only tiny scopes (loop index i, coordinates x and y). No naming convention can replace the code that actually computes the value.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A name does not compute or guarantee a value. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Trusting a descriptive name instead of the code (e.g. assuming average holds the mean although it was never divided): wrong output that the name hides.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Names that differ only in case are different identifiers. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Declaring both count and Count (or total and Total) and updating one while printing the other.
wrong: Writing 7 or 0.0825 directly in formulas is as clear as using a named constant. | right: Give fixed values a final, UPPER_CASE name and use the name.
wrong: Uses abbreviated names such as c or s for a variable whose role is not a temporary loop counter (e.g. c for a count). | right: Use names that indicate what the variables mean.
